It started with a fire drill

In March, our SOC watched a phishing-as-a-service operation turn Railway, a developer cloud platform with a spotless IP reputation, into a token-harvesting engine. Device code phishing lures hit 344 organizations across five countries in under three weeks. Microsoft had no reason to score those logins as risky. That was the whole point.

So we did something we'd never done before. We hand-built a Conditional Access policy blocking Railway's IP ranges, validated it against 14 days of fleet traffic, and pushed it to every eligible Managed ITDR tenant. It stopped 305 attack attempts at the door. Zero legitimate logins were affected.

Then the attackers moved to new infrastructure. They always do.

That's the problem we built Adversary Infrastructure to solve. It's the newest capability in Huntress Managed ITDR, and it turns that one-time emergency response into continuous protection. When one tenant gets hit, every tenant gets the block. We call it herd immunity for identity.

Attackers are renting clean infrastructure and scaling with AI

The Railway campaign told us something about how identity attacks work now. Across 344 victims, we found no two identical phishing lures. Each one was tailored enough to slip past email filtering. That kind of variety at that kind of volume means automation or AI is writing the lures. The group behind it, EvilTokens, sells a storefront with AI workflows for bypassing filters, personalizing pretexts, and hunting inboxes for wire fraud targets. It even has a 24/7 support desk.

The infrastructure side has changed too. Attackers don't need to buy bulletproof hosting anymore. They rent clean, cheap, trusted cloud space, stand up a token relay in minutes, and tear it down when it's burned. Developer platforms, VDI tunnels, and AiTM relays all look legitimate to Microsoft's risk scoring until someone proves otherwise.

The scale is hard to overstate. In a single 14-day window, 5,086 distinct attacker IP addresses hit the Huntress fleet. Partners can't curate blocklists at that pace. Nobody can, by hand.

What Adversary Infrastructure is

Adversary Infrastructure blocks attackers at the Microsoft 365 sign-in, before they ever get a session.

Figure 1: Adversary Infrastructure in the Huntress Platform

When the Huntress SOC confirms the hosting, relay, or proxy infrastructure behind a compromise in one tenant, we turn it into a blocking Conditional Access policy in every eligible, opted-in tenant. Attacks from that infrastructure fail at sign-in instead of becoming incidents you have to clean up.

It's precision blocking, sourced from real attacks we've already investigated across the 17M+ identities we protect. Only the IP ranges that are bad, nothing else. Huntress maintains it end to end. There's no blocklist for you to curate, no policy for you to write, no threat feed for you to consume. And it's included in Managed ITDR for Microsoft 365 at no extra cost.

How it works

The whole loop runs from one confirmed incident to fleet-wide blocking, often the same day.

The SOC confirms a compromise with a real incident in a real tenant, with the hosting, relay, or proxy addresses behind it.

Detection engineers validate the infrastructure. It has to be datacenter or hosting space, scoped tightly to the evidence, with zero legitimate logins anywhere across the fleet and confirmed reports from at least two unrelated partners. A second engineer reviews every nomination. If real users log in from an address, it doesn't ship.

Huntress deploys the block. New campaigns go to our own canary tenants first. Then one blocking policy with one named location per campaign - each labeled [HUNTRESS] - roll out to every eligible, opted-in tenant.

Figure 2: Conditional Access policies by campaign in Adversary Infrastructure

The next attack fails at sign-in. No token is issued. The attack never becomes an incident.

You get the receipt. Every block produces a Low severity incident report naming the targeted identity, source, and campaign, and the credential the attacker tried to use gets rotated.

We check every tenant daily, repair drift, and update ranges as attackers rotate. We never touch policies you authored. Tenants that can't run Conditional Access still get the same detections and incident reports, just after the sign-in instead of before.

Two campaigns that brought you Adversary Infrastructure

Every campaign we've turned into fleet-wide protection started as somebody's very bad day. Here are two.

LSHIY LLC: 81 million login attempts from one IPv6 range. Three months after Railway, our SOC spotted a password spray replaying validated credentials through ROPC, a legacy auth flow that skips the MFA prompt entirely. It compromised 78 accounts across 64 organizations. Here's the part that stung: 55 of those accounts had active Conditional Access policies requiring MFA. The policies looked right. They just didn't cover the flow the attacker used. LSHIY is now a live Adversary Infrastructure campaign. The next tenant that range touches blocks it at sign-in, whether or not its MFA policy has a gap.

1337 Services GmbH: ten weeks of token replay. Between July and September, an attacker captured sessions through AiTM relays and replayed the stolen tokens from a German hosting provider's 193.26.115[.]0/24 IP range. We responded at 79 organizations: 497 successful sign-ins against more than 200,000 failed attempts. The operator rotated through six addresses in that range, one after another, with quiet periods between phases. A block written for one address did nothing against the next. Microsoft flagged them individually. Range-level blocking, maintained by Huntress and updated as the attacker moves, is built for exactly this pattern.

In both cases, the first tenants hit paid the price of cleanup: rogue devices, wiped MFA methods, hidden inbox rules, a payroll email sent to an outside CPA. With Adversary Infrastructure, the next tenant never gets that far.

Where Managed ISPM fits

If you're wondering why Conditional Access blocks live in ITDR when Managed ISPM already manages Conditional Access, here's the clean answer.

ISPM is posture. It deploys broad, durable controls that close whole classes of attack: block device code flow, restrict legacy auth and ROPC, require MFA for all apps. These controls aren't aimed at any one adversary. They're the baseline, and they stay in place. Every policy runs in Learning Mode for 14 days first, so nothing breaks.

Adversary Infrastructure is response. It's narrowly scoped to the exact IP ranges behind incidents the SOC has already reported. It changes as campaigns rotate. Every block fires an incident report. Blocking device code flow is an ISPM policy. Going after Railway is an ITDR policy. Both are Conditional Access, doing different jobs.

They're also better together. ISPM built the plumbing and the expertise to deploy Conditional Access across thousands of tenants without locking anyone out. That's what let us turn the Railway response into a product at all. Posture closes the door. Response catches whoever's still trying the handle.

Already using Managed ITDR? Turn Adversary Infrastructure on to unlock this new protection

Adversary Infrastructure is live in Managed ITDR for Microsoft 365 starting today, November 5.

Existing ITDR partners are opted out by default and can turn it on from the ITDR settings page. Partners onboarding from today forward are opted in by default. Eligible tenants need Entra ID P1 or P2 (Business Premium, or E3 with P1, and up), Security Defaults off, and a healthy, fully onboarded tenant in Huntress.

You must be opted in to be protected, and every tenant you opt in strengthens the herd.

Title: Refreshing the 555 Benchmark for Cloud Detection and Response in the AI era
Context: It used to take attackers days to conduct reconnaissance, lateral movement, and exploitation, but now it only requires a few minutes
Full Text:
How long does it take your security teams to detect a threat, correlate and contextualize relevant data, and take action? For most organizations, the honest answer is still measured in hours or days. Mature organizations are actively working toward reducing that time to minutes, and the most innovative teams are moving to sub-minute timescales using agentic AI.

The reality is that attackers don’t wait. Researchers across the industry, like the Sysdig Threat Research Team, have continuously shown that cloud attacks unfold in 10 minutes or less, and with AI and agentic workflows, the window for defense continues to shrink.

In mid-July 2026, Hugging Face disclosed a security incident unlike anything the industry had documented before. An agentic security research harness breached their production infrastructure. This harness was later confirmed to be part of OpenAI’s internal cyber-capability evaluation. Hugging Face logged more than 17,000 recorded events before the agents were contained, and they deployed LLM-driven analysis agents to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, and map the credentials touched. It took an AI to catch an AI.

Just one month prior, the Sysdig TRT documented JADEPUFFER, which targeted AI and ML infrastructure with purpose-built ransomware. The attacker was also an agent with no human at the keyboard.

These are not isolated incidents; they are the new normal. AI-assisted attacks have compressed the kill chain, and frontier AI models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos have uncovered thousands of new vulnerabilities, too. It used to take attackers days to conduct reconnaissance, lateral movement, and exploitation, but now it only requires a few minutes.

“Cloud threats aren’t just fast; they are automated. Without real-time visibility, an attacker can move from a container escape to resource hijacking in minutes, spiking your compute costs before your team even receives an alert. Early detection is the only way to intercept execution before it impacts your bottom line.” — CISO at a Cryptocurrency Exchange and Trading Platform

The 555 Benchmark was designed for this

The 555 Benchmark for Cloud Detection and Response gives organizations a framework to meet this reality: detect threats in 5 seconds, investigate them in 5 minutes, and respond with precision in 5 minutes. And with agentic capabilities in the hands of defenders, meeting that benchmark is more than achievable.

When 555 was first introduced, it was a challenge; something to work toward. The Hugging Face incident, and other reports of agentic threat actors (ATAs), make clear why this benchmark is now a business imperative. When an autonomous system can break out and breach a production infrastructure via the fastest path, our concern is no longer whether AI can find vulnerabilities. It is whether organizations have continuous visibility into what attackers can reach, what they did, and how quickly they can be stopped. That is exactly what 555 operationalizes.

Ultimately, the 555 Benchmark isn’t a product or quick fix to implement, but a call to action to pressure-test your security processes against the speed of modern attacks. By continuously improving and modernizing your people, processes, and tooling, and by supplementing them with well-governed agentic AI security capabilities, you can reduce the risk of material breach, reputational damage, and financial loss.

Long gone are the days of working to defend your environment over the course of several days. Today, you only have minutes to respond to an attack.

“I don't want to know 15 minutes after someone breached my system. I need to know instantly so we can shut it down before the blast radius expands. To move at the necessary speed, you need to not only be alerted to the right things, but also respond appropriately. Having a benchmark gives us a goal to hold ourselves to.” — Désiré Banse, Former NIST Researcher and Security Operations Manager at a healthcare technology company

Introducing the updated 555 Benchmark Guides for CISOs and practitioners

To help organizations operationalize this framework for the AI era, Sysdig has republished two guides — aimed at different roles working toward the same goal — to support and encourage organizations in striving for 10-minute threat detection and response.

One guide is designed for the practitioners who work in and around the SOC: the security professionals in the trenches and on the front lines. The Hugging Face response team is a model for what this looks like in practice: After the breach was contained, they used agentic AI to do in hours what would’ve taken a team of analysts days. This guide focuses on how to operate at machine speed using the automation, AI tooling, and agentic workflows that make 555 achievable.

“Cloud threat detection and response goes far beyond tooling. You need to implement a specific set of skills and finesse and a different kind of mindset to detect cloud attacks in real time. ”

The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for Cloud Security Practitioners

The other guide is for the CISOs and security leaders who are responsible for leading teams through battle. They own the security strategy and risk, and must report value and breach impact to the board and to other business functions. This guide aligns security outcomes with organizational risk and reflects how, in the AI era, speed is the defining risk factor and defining board-level question.

“For large enterprises, a single hour of downtime costs over $100,000, with industries like finance, healthcare, media, and communications reaching well over $5 million per hour.”

The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for CISOs

Together, these guides provide a framework for security teams and leaders to meet common goals and expectations. It also helps them speak a unified language. By collaborating and following the strategies outlined, they can implement changes that modernize and accelerate cloud security practices, turning what were once ambitious goals into operational reality.

Enterprise security is like a symphony orchestra, with the CISO as the conductor. An oboist cannot sit in for a violinist, and different teams play their own distinct roles. SOC analysts, developers, platform engineers, and business stakeholders each contribute unique skills to the overall composition. Today, AI agents have joined that orchestra — not replacing whole sections, but playing alongside them, automating manual, repetitive processes and handling the parts that move too fast for humans hands alone, so humans can exercise judgment and have a greater impact. Synchronization and speed are survival requirements to maintain a secure and harmonious organization.

What you’ll learn

The updated 555 guides were designed to help organizations mature and modernize detection and response for the AI era through:

Collaboration: Working cross-functionally inside and outside of security and technical teams around shared context and outcomes to enable coordinated, real-time detection and response as humans and automated systems work together.

Integration: Unifying cloud-native telemetry and identity behaviors across cloud, SaaS, and AI systems to build real-time, decision-ready context across your entire environment to enable faster, more accurate detection and response.

Automation: Reducing manual effort across detection, investigation, and response to keep pace with AI-driven attacks by enabling orchestration to execute at machine speed.

Fast and automated incident response = Less attack risk = Lower chance of materiality = Business and operational value of security

If your organization operates in the cloud, now is the time to reassess how fast your security processes actually move. You don’t always need more tools or budget, but you do need the right architecture and better orchestration of the people, processes, and tooling you already have to modernize your cloud threat detection and response and meet the speed that threats demand.

Read and share The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for CISOs and The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for Cloud Security Practitioners today. Attackers are already running at machine speed — it’s time your defense does, too.

Full Text:
Election Day brings typical cyber threats, technical glitches, and misinformation. Hackers tamper with European refrigeration systems. OpenAI faces questions over years of security warnings. Nvidia reportedly restricts business with Chinese data center customers. Binance details a six-billion-dollar heist attributed to North Korea. Barracuda patches critical security flaws. Gartner predicts an engineering-heavy future for security operations. Canadians face charges for hacking U.S. universities. Our guest is Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box, discussing Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. AI takes the pitch, misses the point.

Today is Wednesday November 4th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Election Day 2026 brings a familiar mix of cybersecurity threats, technical glitches, and misinformation.

Election Day 2026 brought a familiar mix of cybersecurity threats, technical glitches, and misinformation. But the biggest technology story emerging from the midterms may be voters' growing resistance to artificial intelligence.

According to Nextgov, election officials reported unsuccessful attempts to penetrate online services, including efforts to guess login credentials. One state election office experienced five spikes in traffic to its ballot drop-box locator, which subsided after officials implemented a CAPTCHA. As of Tuesday evening, election security analysts had received no reports of foreign influence operations.

Meanwhile, ballot scanner malfunctions in New York's Westchester County quickly became fodder for election conspiracy theories. Officials initially attributed rejected ballots to problems with their thickness. Voters were instructed to deposit affected ballots in secure emergency bags for later counting. Despite no evidence of deliberate interference, misleading claims spread rapidly on X, reaching as many as 100 posts per minute.

Beyond election security, voters delivered a significant political setback to the technology industry's ambitious AI expansion.

Axios reports that roughly two dozen ballot measures restricting data center development appeared headed for approval. In Texas, Democratic gubernatorial winner Gina Hinojosa campaigned on maintaining a construction moratorium until lawmakers address environmental and infrastructure concerns.

With Democrats also winning key races in Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona, analysts estimate nearly two-thirds of planned U.S. data center capacity for 2028 could face delays.

The emerging message from voters: They're increasingly concerned about AI's impact on electricity prices, water supplies, and their communities. Silicon Valley may have enormous ambitions, but it turns out the people living next door to those data centers get a vote, too.

Hackers target refrigeration systems across Europe.

Hackers are targeting refrigeration systems across Europe, remotely changing temperature settings and forcing supermarkets to throw away spoiled food.

Attacks reported in November affected stores in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, and Germany, along with food suppliers in the UK. In some cases, attackers switched refrigeration equipment into defrost mode or disabled temperature alarms. Retailers have responded by disconnecting vulnerable equipment from the internet.

The attacks have also raised concerns about medical supplies. In France, hackers reportedly compromised refrigeration equipment supplied to the French Blood Establishment, changing freezer settings from minus 30 degrees Celsius to 110 degrees. An alert technician caught the problem before it disrupted operations, according to French health officials. There's no confirmed loss of blood plasma or harm to patients.

Authorities haven't identified the perpetrators or established whether the incidents are connected. French cybersecurity officials are urging organizations to secure remote access to refrigeration controllers, update firmware, and eliminate default passwords.

The incidents demonstrate how compromising ordinary industrial equipment can have very real physical consequences.

Current and former OpenAI employees say they warned company leadership for years about security weaknesses.

Current and former OpenAI employees say they warned company leadership for years about security weaknesses that could expose sensitive AI research to competitors and foreign governments.

According to Reuters, concerns included broad employee access to internal code repositories, sensitive research documentation, and inadequate security reviews of internal tools. Some employees believed leadership prioritized development speed over security.

Those concerns gained urgency following several incidents, including the arrest of a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a listening device in an executive conference room, and researchers using a rival AI model to access employee accounts and internal systems.

OpenAI disputes suggestions that it neglected security, pointing to restricted repositories, increased investment, and regular reviews. The company reportedly reassigned a quarter of its production engineers to security improvements in August.

The larger challenge: protecting increasingly valuable AI technology without slowing the research that makes it valuable.

Nvidia sets limits on Chinese data center customers.

Nvidia is reportedly imposing new restrictions on data center customers that provide computing services to Chinese companies.

According to the Financial Times, Nvidia has told operators they must limit Chinese customers to no more than 49 percent of their overall business, with the remaining 51 percent coming from non-Chinese companies.

The policy would require data center operators to track how much business they conduct with Chinese firms, potentially complicating operations for providers serving customers in both China and elsewhere.

The Financial Times says Nvidia's sales representatives and regional teams have communicated the restrictions directly to customers, but the company apparently hasn't issued formal written documentation.

The reported move introduces a new limitation on how Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure can be used, adding another consideration for data center operators navigating business relationships with China.

Binance describes the $6 billion North Korean heist.

North Korea has launched several missiles toward the sea, hours after rejecting FBI accusations that its hackers stole more than six billion dollars from cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

The FBI attributes the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Pyongyang denies responsibility and says the accusations undermine prospects for renewed diplomacy with Washington.

Meanwhile, Binance has revealed how the attack unfolded. Hackers spent months compromising three engineers' computers, using malicious software disguised as developer tools and a fake job interview featuring a rigged coding assignment.

Attackers also exploited an internal AI tool to expand their access, eventually reaching Binance's wallet signing infrastructure. The company hasn't explained precisely how the AI tool was abused.

Binance says approximately $2.85 billion in stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted, and affected systems have been rebuilt.

Barracuda patches Email Security Gateway vulnerabilities.

Barracuda Networks is urging customers to patch two vulnerabilities in its Email Security Gateway appliances that could allow attackers to execute commands with root privileges.

One critical flaw enables unauthorized changes to global configurations, while the second allows users with administrator permissions to inject operating system commands.

Barracuda says attackers must first reach the devices’ administrative interfaces. Chaining the vulnerabilities could allow them to bypass authorization controls and gain root access.

The company has released patches and recommends updating firmware, applying security fixes, and restricting administrative access to trusted internal networks.

Gartner predicts SOCs will shift toward more engineers.

By 2028, security operations centers could employ 50 percent more engineers than analysts, according to a new Gartner report. The shift reflects AI's growing ability to handle routine security alerts, freeing human analysts to focus on investigating cases, making decisions, and coordinating responses.

Gartner predicts SOCs won't necessarily shrink. Instead, engineers will increasingly build, test, and refine AI workflows, while analysts expand into threat hunting and exposure management.

The transition creates challenges for entry-level analysts, who traditionally learned their craft by processing alerts. Organizations will need new approaches to training and developing expertise.

Gartner also recommends replacing traditional alert-volume metrics with measures of case accuracy and decision quality.

By 2030, the firm expects SOCs to become more proactive, continuously testing their own defenses rather than primarily responding to alerts.

Canadians are indicted for allegedly hacking U.S. universities.

Two Canadian men have been indicted for allegedly hacking U.S. universities to steal data and mine cryptocurrency.

Prosecutors say Ryan James Roach and Mathiew James Stubbings targeted institutions in four states between 2016 and 2019, deploying malware, stealing credentials, and exploiting university supercomputers. They allegedly used servers registered under false identities and compromised systems to conceal their activities.

Roach has been extradited to the United States, while Stubbings awaits extradition. Both face up to ten years in prison and fines of $250,000 if convicted.

The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an AI provider.

What is ISO/IEC 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for artificial intelligence. Where ISO/IEC 27001 focuses on information security, ISO/IEC 42001 focuses on how an organization governs AI. What exactly does “governing AI” mean? Essentially, it means how AI risks and impacts are assessed, how data is managed, how systems are monitored once they’re in production, and how humans stay in the loop across the AI lifecycle.

This certification means an accredited third party has audited our AIMS and confirmed that it aligns to the standard. To note, this isn’t a one-time exercise, as the certification is maintained through annual surveillance audits. This means our AI governance program is held to the standard for as long as the certificate is active.

Why is ISO/IEC 42001 certification important?

AI is continually evolving how security teams work, and it’s also causing teams to reconsider the questions they ask their vendors. Where does the model come from? What data does it use? Who reviews its outputs? How do we maintain the integrity and quality of our AI products?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification gives customers independent evidence that Rapid7 has a management system in place to address those questions. It demonstrates that the in-scope AI systems are developed and operated under a structured program covering risk assessment, transparency, human oversight, and accountability.

It also supports customers in their own governance work. Many organizations are building AI risk into their third party risk programs and preparing for frameworks and regulations such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act. A vendor's certified AIMS doesn't replace a customer's own due diligence, but it provides a credible, audited starting point.

As with cloud security, AI follows a shared responsibility model. Rapid7 is certified in the role of an AI provider, meaning we’re accountable for how we design, build, and operate these AI systems. Customers remain in control of how they use AI outputs within their own security operations.

Which AI systems are in scope?

The certification covers the AIMS supporting the following AI systems developed within Rapid7 products:

Agentic AI Workflow for MDR (Managed Detection and Response)

AI Dashboard Summary Card (Managed Detection and Response)

AI-Generated Risk Summaries (Exposure Command and Surface Command)

AI-Powered Log Search (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

Attack Surface Management (Surface Command)

ICS Runtime Event Story (InsightCloudSec / Cloud Runtime)

Most of these are capabilities customers use directly within the product. Agentic AI Workflow for MDR supports Rapid7's own SOC analysts as they investigate and respond on behalf of MDR customers.

What's next?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification joins Rapid7's existing security and compliance program, which includes ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2, FedRAMP, IRAP, ENS, BSI C5, as well as U.S. and international cybersecurity regulations. Each is independently assessed against its own defined scope, with details available in the Rapid7 Trust Center (reach out to your Account Executive for access).

Title: Researchers Uncover Prompt Adware Hidden in OpenAI Codex Jailbreak Toolkit
Context: " As of writing, the repository has been forked 77 times and starred 403 times since it was made available on July 10, 2026
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an OpenAI Codex jailbreak bundle that's designed to modify an artificial intelligence (AI) agent's trusted instructions to insert advertisements for a third-party AI gateway.

The phenomenon has been codenamed prompt adware by Check Point Research.

Called Haiou (meaning Seagull in Chinese), the jailbreak modifies OpenAI Codex's configuration files to inject advertisements for the jailbreak author's website into subsequent agent responses.

"The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider," Check Point Research said in a technical report. "The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service."

Adware is a type of software that displays unwanted advertisements, which can appear on users' computers or mobile devices, often in the form of pop-ups or banners. Prompt adware extends this sketchy behavior to AI agents by means of a jailbreak that defeats the model's safety training and content guardrails.

The idea is to persistently modify the agent's global instructions through natural language to influence future responses. This, in turn, causes common greetings or activation words like "Seagull," "hi," "hello," "hey," "yo," and "are you there?" to trigger an advertisement for "zz.aiapi2025[.]top."

Haiou attempts to jailbreak a model by using several prompt injection techniques, such as role-playing and reframing cybersecurity-related requests into a Capture The Flag (CTF) scenario. In addition, it installs security-focused skills devoted to penetration testing, cracking, and reverse engineering.

However, it doesn't stop there. The bundle also injects persistent ads into the global agent instruction file to promote the LLM gateway website. On GitHub, "haiou-codex" is advertised as a "local enhancement configuration package" that adds a "Chinese technical personality and security research workflow to Codex." As of writing, the repository has been forked 77 times and starred 403 times since it was made available on July 10, 2026.

It's worth noting that Codex is not officially available in mainland China, suggesting that the service is likely aimed at individuals or organizations wanting to try out Western AI coding assistants.

What's more, the jailbreak has been bundled within Codex-X, an open-source Chinese visualization tool for configuring Codex through a graphical user interface.

"The behavior is introduced through natural-language instructions and configuration, rather than a traditional executable payload that users and security teams may more readily recognize as software behavior," Pedro Drimel Neto, malware analysis team leader at Check Point, said.

While serving an ad may seem relatively harmless in the larger scheme of things, the findings demonstrate how a bad actor could introduce undesirable behavior through third-party skills or configurations, leading to supply chain attacks.

"As AI agents become part of enterprise environments, the prompts, Skills and third-party components influencing their behavior become part of the trust chain too," Neto said.

The AI Era Is a Container Era

The AI era isn’t arriving on bare metal. It’s arriving on Kubernetes. Model training pipelines, inference services, vector databases, and the agentic workloads that orchestrate them are being built as containers and scheduled across clusters that scale up and down by the minute. The unit of compute is no longer the server. It’s the container, and the node it happens to be running on right now.

That shift changes the math for security teams. The attack surface is no longer a fleet of servers you can enumerate and patch on a monthly cycle. It’s a fleet of nodes that may exist for hours, boot into operating systems that don’t allow you to install a package, and host workloads that move between them without warning. Every one of those nodes is a host, and every host operating system carries its own vulnerabilities and its own configuration risk, regardless of what’s running in the containers above it.

Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS) extends build-to-runtime coverage for images, containers, and serverless workloads.

The Problem: Host Security Wasn’t Built for Container Platforms

For years, securing a host meant one thing: install an RPM or a DEB on it. That model worked when hosts were long-lived and homogeneous. It breaks down in container platforms in two ways.

Container-optimized operating systems don’t accept packages. AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS (COS), Red Hat CoreOS, and their peers deliberately lock down the root filesystem and remove the package manager. There’s nothing to yum install. Security tooling has to run the way everything else on these nodes runs: as a container.

Package-based deployment doesn’t fit orchestrated environments. Kubernetes teams manage everything through manifests, Helm charts, and GitOps pipelines. A security agent that has to be installed out of band, node by node, is the one thing on the cluster that isn’t declared, versioned, and reconciled like everything else. It also can’t keep up: a node pool that scales from ten nodes to two hundred during a training run needs security coverage on every node it creates, automatically.

The result is a coverage gap at the foundation. Teams invest in scanning container images and monitoring running containers, and rightly so. But the container runtime, the kubelet, the kernel, and every system library sit on the host OS. If that layer is unmonitored, a clean image running on a vulnerable node is still a vulnerable workload.

The Solution: Qualys Cloud Agent as a Container Image

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image, published directly to Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher account. It runs on every node in your cluster as a DaemonSet and delivers the same host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit that the Qualys Cloud Agent provides on any other platform, without touching the host’s package manager.

The image ships with the Qualys Cloud Agent pre-installed and dynamically pulls down the components it needs at runtime, such as application manifests and supporting utilities, so it stays lightweight while remaining fully functional. Because it’s deployed through Kubernetes, the orchestrator does the work your provisioning scripts used to do: every node that joins the cluster gets an agent, and every node that leaves takes its agent with it.

Combined with TotalCloud KCS, the Containerized Cloud Agent gives you full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane, for vulnerabilities, audit, and posture, as well as runtime security, drift, and threat detection.

Full Host Coverage for Container-Optimized and Immutable Operating Systems

Immutable operating systems are the right choice for container platforms: a smaller attack surface, atomic updates, and a root filesystem that can’t drift. But immutability cuts both ways. If you can’t install anything, you can’t install a traditional agent, and many teams have run these nodes blind. The Containerized Cloud Agent closes that gap. It runs as a privileged container with the host mounts it needs to assess the underlying OS, so Bottlerocket, COS, and CoreOS nodes get the same vulnerability and compliance visibility as a conventional Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) server, with no changes to the host image and no compromise to the immutability that made you choose that OS in the first place.

Your Choice of Agent on Mutable Linux, Too

The Containerized Cloud Agent isn’t limited to immutable operating systems. Previously, a RHEL or Ubuntu node meant installing the RPM or DEB package, full stop. Now you choose. Teams with a mix of virtual machines (VMs) and containers can keep the package on VMs and use the Containerized Cloud Agent on cluster nodes. Teams that are all-in on Kubernetes can standardize on the Containerized Cloud Agent everywhere and never manage a host package again. Either way, the data lands in the same place, with the same detections and the same TruRisk scoring.

Deployment That Fits How You Already Run Kubernetes

The Containerized Cloud Agent is a DaemonSet, which means the orchestrator guarantees one agent per node, on every node, for the life of the cluster. Autoscaling node pools, spot instances that get reclaimed, and cluster upgrades that replace every node are all handled without a ticket, a script, or a human. Coverage becomes a property of the cluster rather than a task someone has to remember.

Because it’s delivered as a Helm chart and YAML manifests, the agent lives in the same GitOps repository as your workloads. Upgrading is a tag change and a pull request. Rolling back is a revert. Node selectors and tolerations let you target specific pools, and the same manifest works across dev, staging, and production. Security stops being the exception to your deployment model.

One Image Across Every Operating System

You don’t need a Bottlerocket build, a CoreOS build, and an Ubuntu build. A single Containerized Cloud Agent image runs across all supported operating systems. That collapses your deployment matrix: one image to vet through your supply-chain controls, one image to pin and version, one DaemonSet manifest to maintain. When a new agent release ships, it’s one tag to update across the entire estate. Images that comply with Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) are available for environments that require them.

Complete Coverage Across Intel and ARM

Cluster node pools increasingly mix x86 and ARM instances, with Graviton, Cobalt, and Axion sitting alongside traditional Intel and AMD nodes. Images are published for both Intel/x64 and ARM, so a multi-architecture cluster gets consistent coverage without special-casing by pool.

Container risk doesn’t live in one layer. It spans the cloud account the cluster runs in, the node operating systems, the Kubernetes control plane and its configuration, the images in your registries, the containers running in production, and the identities and network paths that connect all of it. Securing any one of those layers in isolation leaves you with a partial view and a false sense of coverage. TotalCloud is built to cover all of them on one platform, with one risk score.

In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time.

In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use.

For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. The population overview page shows which personal agents are active across your users and how many accounts use them, so you can determine whether agent traffic is a meaningful part of your business. Every login and sign-up event now shows whether a personal agent made the request, and which one. Fraud teams can filter accounts by AI assistant events or number of AI assistants.

Additionally, each user's account overview shows the agents acting for that account. A fraud analyst investigating an unusual login can tell whether it came from an agent the customer has relied on for weeks, or from an agent that appeared for the first time today and needs a closer look. If it looks like an attacker is using an agent on an account, fraud analysts can mitigate that account directly, with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID, without blocking the agent for everyone else who relies on it.

Together, these views give you a clearer basis for deciding which personal agents to welcome, limit, or block.

Set access policies that reflect your preferences

We introduced AI bot policies this summer so site owners could make separate access control choices for AI bots used for Search, Training, and Agent behaviors. Now we’re expanding the existing Agents policy to include granular control options for supported personal agents. To reflect this broader scope, we’re renaming the setting AI Crawler and Agent access policies.

In Security Settings, you can set an overall Agents policy, then choose a different policy for each supported personal agent: Allow (do not block), Block on pages with ads, or Block. For example, you can set the overall Agents policy to Block on pages with ads, then choose Allow (do not block) for a supported personal agent you want to welcome. Your existing Search and Training policies stay as they are.

You can also make these choices when you add a new zone to Cloudflare. During onboarding, we ask whether you monetize pages with ads and then tailor the recommended policies to your answer. You can always revisit your access controls later in Security Settings.

The right policy depends on your site. One publisher may allow a supported personal agent throughout its site so readers can find its articles, while another may block that same agent on pages where ads support the content. Both publishers are choosing the access control that works for their business.

Agent identity is only part of the story

The analytics and policies we’re launching today give site owners visibility into personal agent activity and control over their access. Our next goal is to help site owners preserve the context of their relationships with users when personal agents act as intermediaries. A site may recognize the agent making a request but lack information it would otherwise have about the user: whether they are an existing customer, what they authorized the agent to do, whether they have a subscription, or which protections should apply.

Reaching that goal will require privacy-aware ways to (1) carry user context through an agent, (2) help sites assess reputation, and (3) establish clear accountability when something goes wrong. We’ll be sharing more as we work with agent operators and others across the ecosystem, so site owners can choose whether to grant agents greater access while continuing to build relationships with their users.

Make the choice for your site

That person asking a personal agent to compare products, find support, or complete a purchase is still a customer trying to reach your business. Review how personal agents are accessing your site, then visit Security Settings → AI Crawler and Agent access policies to set the terms that work for your site.

Title: Radio With No Radar: Why Agent Runtime Security Fails Without the Layers Beneath It
Context: With more than 280 app integrations, more than 1,000 detection controls and more than 1 million agents detected, Reco brings agent security, posture management and threat...
Full Text:
Nearly every agent security pitch now ends on the same promise: the product stops the bad action in real time. The promise holds for one kind of agent, the kind whose traffic passes through a gateway the enterprise owns. Most agents never touch one.

One recent case shows what that gap looks like in practice. An employee asked an AI assistant to trigger a mass-email automation. The automation hit a recipient-limit policy and failed, so the assistant, which was also connected to the employee's personal mailbox, offered to send the batch from there instead. The employee approved without registering that the assistant was about to route around the sanctioned system. An unknown number of external recipients received email from a personal account rather than the approved channel.

No jailbreak was involved. The assistant did exactly what it was built to do, and the fix was not retraining a model. It was a single runtime rule that blocks any attempt to reach more than fifty external domains and explains to the user what the tool is about to do. Knowing where to apply a rule like that depends on seeing which agents exist, what they are connected to and what normal looks like for each. That visibility is the part most runtime pitches skip.

The runtime is the application, not the pipe

The year's largest agent launches placed agents inside platforms the buyer does not own. Claudeforce runs Claude inside Salesforce's trust boundary, Claude Tag lives inside Slack and Copilot lives inside Microsoft 365. Workday, which says AI now drives more than a quarter of its new annual contract value, runs its agents inside Workday. In each case the agent's tools are the application's features, its knowledge is the application's data and its permissions are the application's permission model.

A gateway can only inspect what passes through it. An agent that runs inside Salesforce, fires from a Flow, reads CRM records and writes case comments sends nothing past an inspection point, and the same is true of a Copilot agent assembling a document from SharePoint or a Slack-native agent reading years of channel history. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 describes this gap as the "unreachable skill" scenario under AST09, No Governance: a capability deployed inside a third-party platform where no external scanner can go.

Security has made a move like this before. Firewalls once inspected packets by source, destination and port, until applications stopped mapping cleanly to ports and malicious traffic began to look identical to legitimate traffic. The inspection point moved up the stack to the application, where the signal lives. Agent runtime needs the same move, with a complication the earlier one never faced: the application layer belongs to someone else. A gateway-only strategy protects the agents an enterprise hosts itself, which are the fewest and the slowest growing.

The inspection point is also a target

In March 2026, attackers compromised LiteLLM, the open-source gateway that routes agent traffic to model providers. The malicious packages were live for about forty minutes, and CloudSEK later put the exposure at more than 2,500 organizations. LiteLLM is the kind of component a security-conscious team adds on purpose to watch AI traffic, which made the inspection point itself the attack vector.

None of this argues against gateways. It argues against treating any single component as the whole strategy. A gateway is more software in the supply chain, with its own release pipeline and dependencies, and it concentrates exactly the traffic an attacker wants. When enforcement is a shared component, its failure is a shared failure.

A millisecond verdict needs a memory

Runtime decisions are made in milliseconds, and the hard cases are the gray ones. A support agent pulling customer data may be doing its job or exfiltrating it. A coding agent reading a repository may be gathering context or performing reconnaissance. A finance agent creating an OAuth connection may be doing integration work or making the first move of a compromise. The action alone does not carry the verdict. The agent's identity and owner, its permissions, its normal behavior, the sensitivity of the data, the destination and the delegation chain behind the request do.

Chains raise the bar. Enforcement that evaluates only the last hop sees an authorized agent performing an action it has permission for, and misses that the authority arrived through a chain nobody approved. Judging the whole chain at runtime means already knowing it, and that knowledge cannot be assembled in a millisecond. Enforcement without that map is an air-traffic controller with a radio but no radar: commands can be issued, but the picture of which plane is headed where does not exist.

What real agent runtime looks like

Three properties follow. Enforcement has to sit where the agents are, across several vantage points such as native platform hooks, API-level controls, the MCP layer, the browser and the endpoint, rather than at a single gateway. Every verdict has to be computed against a live map of identity, permissions, connectivity and activity (IPCA), plus data sensitivity and delegation, which is what turns the gray cases into judgments. And the response menu has to be wider than block.

Mature enforcement is graduated. It allows the known-good, warns where justification is plausible, redacts where the data is the problem and blocks where the chain is hostile. It routes the highest-stakes actions to a human and keeps a kill switch for the provably compromised agent that suspends it, revokes its grants and preserves the trail. Every verdict is logged with its full causal path, because an incident review and a regulator want the same five things: the agent, the chain, the data, the destination and the policy.

Do not buy the end state

Irregular's Dan Lahav calls the mistake the end-state fallacy: assuming the properties of the eventual equilibrium apply to the transition actually underway. In runtime purchasing, it is the belief that inline enforcement will eventually see everything, so the unglamorous layers can be skipped. That end state is not available this year from any vendor at any price. Runtime coverage is partial and platform hooks are arriving unevenly.

What can be bought now, everywhere, is the stack runtime depends on: discovery across every vantage point, posture on every platform, identity and ownership for every agent and context for every decision. Each enforcement point that opens later then snaps into a map that already knows what normal looks like. The full argument for where enforcement belongs is in From AI Runtime to Agent Runtime.

The first ninety days, in order

A sequence that follows the stack bottom-up looks like this.

Window

The work

How to know it is real

Weeks 1 to 2: get the number

Connect what is already running (the identity provider, major platforms, network tools, the email layer) and let discovery work across every vantage point at once. No gateway deployment, no endpoint rollout, no rerouted traffic.

Time to first insight is days, not quarters. The discovered population is several multiples of the list IT keeps.

Weeks 3 to 6: names and configurations

Every discovered agent gets a named human owner or is suspended. Configuration debt is triaged, starting with the platforms hosting the most reachable agents: guest-user exposures, intake features wired to agent triggers, sharing rules from three years ago. Guardrails go on customer-facing and privileged agents first.

A human raises a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?"

Weeks 7 to 12: the queue and the path

Context-aware risk tiering so review starts with the agent that can actually hurt the business, a least-privilege review cadence on the top tier and a sanctioned route for business teams to ship agents with secure defaults.

Any critical rating can be explained as a chain, and builders are offered a path instead of only a block.

The enablement path matters because the builders are coming either way. Blocking teaches evasion, while a good path teaches compliance.

Teams can place themselves with a four-level test. Blind means the board's three questions (how many agents exist, what they can reach and who is accountable) have no current answer. Inventoried means the population is discovered, counted and refreshed continuously. Governed means every agent has an owner, posture is managed against baselines and risk is tiered with context. Instrumented means enforcement operates where agents run, with graduated verdicts and a full causal path in every alert. Most enterprises are at the first level, whatever the policy document says, and a vendor selling instrumentation to a blind organization is selling enforcement that can act but cannot judge.

Seven questions that sort vendors

Every vendor deck now says agent security. These questions separate vendors that built for the problem from vendors that renamed a product, because each is easy to answer well only if the architecture underneath exists.

Ask

What a good answer looks like

Can you find agents that never authenticate through SSO?

Yes, across several independent vantage points, each seeing something the others cannot.

For an agent you rated critical, show me the chain.

A complete, reachable attack path (capability, reachability, asset) that an analyst can verify, not an aggregate score.

Does the same finding produce different severities on different agents?

Yes, demonstrated on a sandboxed agent and a customer-facing one.

When one agent invokes another, can you reconstruct the delegation chain?

Original requester, every hop and the final action. An audit trail that starts at the last agent is not one.

What context feeds an allow, block or redact verdict?

Identity, permissions, delegation and data sensitivity, not the prompt alone.

What happens to my protection if your enforcement component is compromised?

A specific answer that addresses the LiteLLM incident directly.

How long until I see my real agent inventory?

Days. A quarter is a different product.

Platforms built around the map rather than the individual agent can answer these directly. One leading example is Reco, whose Reco Graph connects every human and non-human identity, application, permission and agent action into a single live view, so that reach, not configuration, is the unit of analysis. One measured program that applied this approach moved its posture score from 47% to 91% across 21 platforms in 30 days.

The full ninety-day sequence, the four-level self-assessment and all fifteen vendor questions are in The Agent Security Checklist: Your First 90 Days.

Title: PHP2Shell on Windows and macOS: Automating the PHP Upgrade, With or Without an Agent
Context: PHP has released a critical security update addressing two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (collectively tracked as PHP2Shell), that allow unauthenticated...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) allows unauthenticated remote code execution on exposed PHP servers. PHP has released fixed versions. On Linux, distribution packages carry the fix. On Windows and macOS, they don’t: Microsoft and Apple don’t ship PHP, so the fix is an in-place PHP upgrade that has traditionally been done by hand, one server at a time. Qualys TruRisk Eliminate’s Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) capability runs Qualys TRU-published scripts that upgrade each PHP installation to the latest patch release of its current minor series. On Windows, the script verifies the official build by SHA256 and rolls back on failure. On macOS, it upgrades through Homebrew. If a host is on an end-of-life series, the script stops, reports it, and then you apply the PHP2Shell mitigation script instead. The same script runs through the Cloud Agent or, on hosts without one, through an authenticated Qualys scanner. Agentless runs need a Windows or SSH credential with rights to stop services and replace PHP binaries. Plan a maintenance window for both because IIS, Apache, or php-fpm restarts during the upgrade.

PHP has released a critical security update addressing two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (collectively tracked as PHP2Shell), that allow unauthenticated remote code execution against exposed PHP servers.

On Linux, patching is straightforward: distribution vendors ship updated packages, and Qualys TruRisk Eliminate deploys them.

Windows and macOS are a different story. There is no straightforward vendor patch to deploy, so the fix must be a PHP upgrade, which has traditionally required someone to log in to each server and apply it manually. This blog explains how the Qualys Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) capability in Qualys TruRisk Eliminate closes the gap for both deployment models: agent-based and agentless (scanner-based).

Why Patch Management Can’t Deliver the Fix on Windows and macOS

Patching works by deploying the fix that an operating system or software vendor publishes. For PHP on Windows and macOS, that fix does not exist in a deployable form.

Windows: no official installer or updater. Microsoft does not ship PHP, and PHP does not ship an installer or an in-place updater for Windows. The official builds on downloads.php.net are plain ZIP archives published in multiple flavors (Thread Safe / Non-Thread Safe, x64 / x86, and per Visual Studio compiler). Upgrading means picking the right build, stopping IIS or Apache, replacing the binaries in place while preserving php.ini and custom extensions, and restarting services. Third-party stacks such as XAMPP, WampServer, Laragon, Chocolatey and Scoop each add their own layout on top of that.

macOS: Apple no longer ships PHP. PHP was removed from macOS in Monterey (12.0), and Apple software updates do not touch it. php.net publishes only source code, so on modern Macs, PHP most commonly comes from Homebrew (the php formula or a versioned php@8.x formula).

The result is that a PHP server on Windows or macOS will appear vulnerable, with no corresponding patch in the TruRisk Eliminate patch catalog. The vulnerability is real; the remediation path is not a patch.

Custom Assessment and Remediation Closes the Gap with TruRisk Eliminate

TruRisk Eliminate covers four remediation paths: patch, mitigate, isolate, or run a custom script. PHP on Windows and macOS needs the fourth. The CAR capability in TruRisk Eliminate lets you run controlled remediation scripts on your assets from the same platform that detected the exposure. The Qualys Threat Research Unit (TRU) has published PHP upgrade scripts for Windows and macOS in the CAR library so that every host is upgraded the same way. Search the library for “PHP Update to Latest Patch Version” under the PHP2Shell category and import the script for each platform.

Figure 1: PHP2Shell category in the CAR script library. Figure 2: The PHP Update to Latest Patch Version script in the CAR script library (PHP2Shell category).

Both scripts are built around the same principles:

Upgrade within the installed minor series only. 8.2.33 moves to the latest 8.2.x, 8.4.27 to the latest 8.4.x. The scripts never jump a major or minor version, so applications keep running on the branch they were tested against.

Mitigate what can’t be upgraded. If the installed series is end-of-life and no longer published, the script stops and reports it instead of guessing. For those hosts, deploy the PHP2Shell mitigation script from the CAR library. It applies configuration changes that block the attack path and restarts the affected services. Mitigation reduces the risk until you can move to a supported branch; it doesn’t replace the upgrade.

Windows: Official Builds, Verified and Rolled Back on Failure

Discovers every PHP installation on the host, not just the one on PATH: machine and per-user PATH entries, common folders (C:\php*, XAMPP, WAMP, Laragon, Program Files, Scoop), IIS FastCGI handlers in applicationHost.config, and any Windows service that launches a PHP binary.

Detects each installation’s exact build flavor (TS/NTS, x64/x86, VC15/VS16/VS17) by querying php.exe itself, then selects the matching official build from downloads.php.net/releases.json.

Honours the machine WinHTTP proxy automatically, since the SYSTEM account has no user proxy settings.

Downloads the archive and verifies its SHA256 against the published hash before anything is touched.

Stops IIS (W3SVC/WAS), Apache and any php/php-cgi processes using that directory, takes a full backup of the PHP folder, copies the new binaries over the top (php.ini and extra extensions are preserved), and confirms the new version by running php.exe.

Rolls back from the backup and restarts services automatically if the post-upgrade version check fails.

macOS: Homebrew Upgrades Within the Same PHP Series

The macOS script handles the realities of Homebrew, as follows:

Confirms PHP is present and resolves the real binary through symlinks into the Homebrew Cellar to determine which formula owns it (php or php@8.x). PHP from MacPorts, MAMP or a manual build is reported and left alone.

Runs brew as the user who owns the Homebrew installation, because Homebrew refuses to run as root even though CAR executes as root. It also repairs any Homebrew files left owned by root from earlier runs so brew can write to them.

Refreshes Homebrew with retry handling for the common “another brew update is already running” case, and falls back to cached formula data if the refresh fails.

Stays on the installed series. If the default PHP formula has moved to a newer series (for example, the host is on 8.2.x but PHP now tracks 8.4), the script installs or upgrades PHP 8.2 and relinks the PHP command to it rather than forcing a major upgrade.

Restarts the php-fpm service via brew services if it was running before the upgrade and prints the final php -v so the result is visible in the job output.

Agent or Agentless: The Same Script Reaches Every Host

When you create a script in CAR, you choose how it reaches the host. Agent Devices run the script locally through the installed Cloud Agent. Perimeter Devices require no Cloud Agent. The script is delivered and executed through an authenticated Qualys scanner. The script content is identical in both cases; only the delivery changes. Select Windows or Mac as the platform to match the script.

Figure 3: Creating the script in CAR. Choose Agent Devices or Perimeter Devices (agentless), then select Windows or Mac as the platform.

Agent-Based Remediation

In ETM, identify Windows and macOS hosts flagged for the PHP2Shell CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) and tag them by platform.

In CAR, create or import the Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts with Agent Devices selected and run each against its platform tag.

Schedule the install run in a maintenance window, since IIS, Apache, or php-fpm will be restarted.

Review job results and rescan to confirm the QID closes.

Agentless Remediation

Many exposed PHP servers sit on appliances, DMZ servers, legacy hosts, and systems owned by other teams: a Windows Server in the DMZ running a vendor web application on IIS and PHP, or Mac minis in a build lab owned by engineering. Many can’t run, or aren’t allowed to run, a Cloud Agent.

A network scan can show that these systems are exposed, but remediating them has usually required someone to log in and make changes by hand, one server at a time. With unauthenticated remote code execution on the table, that pace leaves your perimeter open.

With the CAR capability in TruRisk Eliminate, the same Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts run directly on scanner-based hosts through the Perimeter Devices option.

Find your scanner-only hosts. In ETM, identify exposed PHP servers using the PHP2Shell CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619).

Create the scripts for Perimeter Devices. In the CAR module of TruRisk Eliminate, select the PHP upgrade script for the host’s platform from the library, choose Perimeter Devices and Windows or Mac, and point it at the scanner appliance that can reach those hosts with the appropriate authentication records (Windows or SSH).

Run the job. Launch the job against your scanner-based hosts. The scripts behave identically whether launched from an agent or a scanner.

Confirm the remediation. Review the job output for the recorded before/after version on each host, then rerun the scan and confirm the QID no longer reports.

What the Job Output Looks Like

Each host returns a short, readable log entry with the execution status and the before/after PHP versions. Below, a scanner-based macOS host is upgraded from PHP 8.2.33 to 8.2.35 within the 8.2 series, with the php@8.2 formula relinked as the active PHP.

Figure 4: CAR job results showing the PHP upgrade output on a scanner-based macOS host.

On Windows, the log additionally lists every PHP installation discovered on the host, the detected build flavor, SHA256 verification, the services stopped and restarted, and the backup folder location.

Figure 5: CAR job results showing the PHP upgrade output on a scanner-based Windows host.

Conclusion

PHP2Shell is a reminder that remediation goes beyond patching. When there is no straightforward vendor patch to deploy, you still need a safe, fast way to close the exposure. With TruRisk Eliminate, you can discover every PHP installation, upgrade it to the latest release of its current series with integrity verification, automatic rollback, and service restart, and do it from the same console that detected the exposure, agentless on scanner-only hosts and through the Cloud Agent where it is installed.

Qualys customers can find the Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts, along with the PHP2Shell mitigation script, in the CAR script library. Review the CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) in ETM and begin with your internet-facing perimeter.

Not a Qualys customer? Access Qualys’ free PHP2Shell mitigation service to help protect your environment against this threat.

Sign Up for Free Mitigation Service

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Will the script jump me from PHP 8.2 to 8.4?

No. It upgrades only within the installed minor series. 8.2.33 moves to the latest 8.2.x. Applications stay on the branch they were tested against.

What happens on an end-of-life series?

The script stops and reports it. Deploy the PHP2Shell mitigation script until you can move to a supported branch.

Does this work without a Cloud Agent?

Yes. Choose Perimeter Devices and run the same script through an authenticated Qualys scanner. You need a Windows or SSH credential with rights to stop services and replace PHP binaries.

What does the Windows script verify?

It detects the build flavor, downloads the matching official build from downloads.php.net, verifies SHA256 before anything is touched, and rolls back from a full backup if the post-upgrade version check fails.

Full Text:
The browser has become a critical enterprise attack surface. Employees rely on the browser to access business applications, interact with AI tools, and handle sensitive data. Knowing this, attackers seek to exploit browser sessions for credential theft and data exfiltration.

Today, CrowdStrike Falcon® Seraphic® Enterprise Browser is natively available on the CrowdStrike Falcon platform, extending protection into the browser. Security teams can manage browser security alongside existing Falcon capabilities through a unified platform experience. This provides a simpler way to protect browser activity across managed and unmanaged devices, without requiring employees to adopt a dedicated enterprise browser or reroute traffic.

The availability of Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser on the Falcon platform delivers three key advantages:

Less to manage: Browser security, secure remote access, and BYOD/contractor access are managed directly within the organization’s Falcon platform environment.

Faster to deploy: Protection works in the browsers teams already use; there is no need to deploy a dedicated browser or reroute traffic.

Coverage where the sensor can't go: Protection extends to unmanaged, BYOD, and contractor devices without mobile device management (MDM) enrollment.

Stop Browser-Based Threats, Protect Data, and Secure Access

Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser provides real-time security controls inside browser sessions, where users access applications, handle sensitive data, and interact with AI tools. Its browser-layer capabilities address five important use cases:

Blocking browser-based attacks: Runtime inspection helps detect and disrupt malicious browser activity, including phishing, ClickFix, malicious scripts, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks.

Identity and session protection: Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser extends protection beyond authentication to help stop session token theft and session hijacking within active browser sessions.

Data and AI controls at the point of use: Teams can enforce policies on browser actions such as copy, paste, upload, and download; this helps prevent sensitive data from reaching unsanctioned web applications and generative AI tools.

Browser extension management: Security teams can inventory browser extensions, evaluate their risk, and enforce policies that allow or block risky extensions across supported browsers.

Secure access to private applications: Policy-controlled access to internal web applications and resources is provided for employees and contractors, including on unmanaged devices, without relying on traditional VPN or VDI for supported workflows.

Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser complements the broader security context of the Falcon platform. With browser telemetry available in CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM, analysts can search, investigate, and correlate browser activity with endpoint, identity, and third-party data to accelerate triage and response. With richer context and more places to act, security teams can follow the adversary rather than the boundaries between products.

Title: Barracuda’s security appliances have a security problem of their own
Context: The company has disclosed two critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that, if chained together, could allow threat actors to bypass authorization controls and gain root...
Full Text:
Barracuda, which offers a wide variety of cybersecurity devices, has been bitten by a bug itself.

The company has disclosed two critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that, if chained together, could allow threat actors to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to devices.

They consist of a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (rated a critical 9.3 severity on the common vulnerability scoring system), and a command injection vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-111560 (rated an 8.6 high-severity on CVSS). Attackers need to have access to the admin interface of a susceptible device to successfully exploit these vulnerabilities.

Barracuda has released security patches, which it advises customers to apply immediately.

The vulnerabilities impact numerous popular Barracuda products

Root access on an email gateway puts the attacker in the place that every inbound and outbound message passes, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. It may also expose the credentials and connections the gateway uses to reach the mail server and directory. “Those are the keys to the kingdom, if you will,” he said.

CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 both impact Barracuda’s Email Security Gateway (ESG), but CVE-2026-111560 also impacts its Web Security Gateway (WSG), Web Application Firewall (WAF), WAF Control Center (WCC), Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC), and Message Archiver (BMA), the company said.

Customers using these products should verify that their systems are running the latest firmware versions and have received all security patches, it advised. The device will show the latest firmware version available; if a device’s firmware is multiple versions out of date, users may need to perform several updates.

Enterprises whose appliances’ admin interfaces are not publicly accessible from the web are less exposed, Barracuda said; the company advised restricting access to these interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls to limit exposure.

“The biggest concern is how these two vulnerabilities could chain together,” said Jon Nelson, principal advisory director at Infotech, noting that an attacker who can bypass authentication and then exploit command injection could move from accessing an exposed appliance to executing commands on it. “Assessing each vulnerability in isolation can understate the risk,” he said.

Dickson added that security leaders should read the advisory closely, as it calls one flaw “pre-authentication,” then lists “Authentication Required: Yes, administrative access.”

“Both cannot be true in the usual sense,” he pointed out. Likely access here means being able to reach the admin interface over the network, without a password.

“If your admin interface faces the internet, that condition is already met,” Dickson said.

The advisory also labels a 9.3 severity rating as “high,” when 9.0 and above is actually “critical” on the standard scale, he pointed out. “These are small things, but labels drive patching queues,” he noted. Also, the advisory does not say whether these flaws are currently being exploited, but it does not say they are not, either.

How enterprises should respond

“Get the admin interface off the internet,” Dickson emphasized, noting that, as a cybersecurity consultant, he gives that advice at least a handful of times a week. “Management interfaces on edge devices are continually a source of vulnerability.”

Once teams limit admin access to a trusted internal network or a dedicated management network, Dickson advised, they should then “verify the patch rather than assume it was properly installed.” From there, he said, analyze for unauthorized visitors by reviewing admin logs, check for unfamiliar accounts, and look for unexpected outbound connections from the device.

History matters here, he added. In 2023, after a zero-day on this same email security gateway (ESG), Barracuda told customers with compromised appliances to replace them outright rather than rely on the patch. As he put it: “A patch fixes the lock. It does not tell you who already has a key.”

Nelson agreed that enterprises should look closely at who can reach their administrative interfaces. They should, in addition, put access behind additional controls such as a properly configured zero trust access layer.

“Exposing those interfaces directly to the internet was always a bad idea,” he said. “As AI makes it easier to find weaknesses and chain attacks together, that exposure becomes increasingly difficult to justify.” AI is also expanding the search for software flaws to include issues such as business logic weaknesses where an application can be made to bypass its intended controls. Authentication and authorization bypasses deserve particular attention in that context, Nelson said.

As more vendors use advanced AI to examine their code, CISOs should prepare for more flaw disclosures and potentially shorter windows to respond to them, he noted. “That means identifying exposed appliances, restricting access, and having a response plan ready before the next zero day arrives,” he said.

Understanding what each appliance exposes

Security appliances are increasingly creating vulnerabilities in corporate networks, which is changing the cybersecurity discussion. Enterprises rely on them to protect the network, yet ultimately they are software systems with vulnerabilities of their own.

“They sit exactly where attackers want to be,” Dickson noted.

Firewalls, VPNs, and email gateways face the internet by design; that is their job, he said. They see sensitive traffic and hold credentials. Most cannot run the endpoint detection tools that protect laptops and servers, so a compromise can remain undetected for a long time, and every customer runs the same firmware, so one working exploit can scale to thousands of organizations.

“The discussion is shifting from which box to buy to what the box itself exposes,” Dickson said. “Every appliance purchase is a decision to trust a vendor’s code at the most exposed point in the network.” It deserves the same scrutiny as any other in an enterprise, he noted.

Buyers should ask their vendors four questions, he advised: Is the admin interface exposed to the internet by default; how quickly do patches ship; are they applied automatically; and what logging can users see?

“The security appliance does not just protect the perimeter,” Dickson pointed out. “It is the perimeter, and it should be treated as the most attacked system an organization owns, because it is.”
